summary:
VisualFire is a web tool for exploring satellite fire detections from 2000 to today, built on a harmonized MODIS and VIIRS dataset served by a FastAPI and DuckDB backend. It brings four views together in one interface: an interactive map and table of individual detections colored by sensor, a multi-year calendar with charts of confidence, day and night, satellites and fire source type, a years by months (or years by weeks) matrix of the full series, and an anomaly view that compares any month with the historical median of a zone, either a country or the visible map area. That last view adds a traffic-light rating and cumulative-season curves plotted against the historical range, and every view can be exported to CSV or PNG.

By harmonizing both sensors into a single schema, with consistent confidence levels, pixel area and fire radiative power, we can build one continuous 25-year series instead of two incompatible ones. This lets researchers see the seasonal pattern at a glance, identify which months and years had the most fire, and tell whether the current month or season is normal, above normal or extreme for a given zone.

This matters because it turns hundreds of millions of raw detections into a direct answer to the question of whether a fire season is unusual. That supports early warning, risk assessment and climate research.
details:
Visual Fire lets a researcher explore two decades of satellite fire detections in one place and judge whether a given month or season is unusual. The user picks a filter such as country, minimum confidence or day versus night, and the tool shows the detections on an interactive map linked to a table, a multi-year calendar that places the same month side by side for several years on a shared color scale, and a set of charts covering confidence, day and night, satellites and fire source type. A further view arranges the whole 2000-to-today series as a matrix of years by months or years by weeks, colored by raw value, by anomaly relative to the typical month, or by a traffic-light rating. For any month, the tool computes the historical median and typical range for the same zone, which can be a country or simply the area currently visible on the map. It reports how many times above or below that median the month is, and it assigns a green, yellow, orange or red status. It also draws the cumulative season against the historical band, so a user can see at a glance whether the year is running ahead of or behind normal. Results can be exported as CSV, and each chart can be saved as an image.

Under the hood, the harmonized MODIS and VIIRS detections are stored as Parquet files partitioned by year and queried with DuckDB through a FastAPI service written in Python. The service exposes endpoints for paginated detections, daily calendar aggregates, chart statistics, a streamed CSV export, and a complete daily series that is computed once per set of filters and then held in memory. The front end is a single page of plain JavaScript that uses Leaflet for the map, with OpenStreetMap, CARTO and Esri satellite imagery as base layers, and Chart.js for the charts. Everything runs on an ordinary laptop with no special hardware.

The main benefit is that it turns a very large collection of individual detections into an answer a non-specialist can read quickly, without GIS software or custom scripts. We hope it helps researchers, environmental agencies and communicators spot abnormal fire seasons early, compare regions and years fairly, and share reproducible figures and data.

Several design decisions came from the team's concerns about interpreting this kind of data correctly. VIIRS finds more fires because of its finer resolution, so raw counts jump when it joins the series. For that reason the tool also offers fire radiative power and pixel area as metrics that depend less on the sensor, and it warns users about the effect. The median is used instead of the mean so that a few extreme years do not distort the baseline, and zones with a median of zero are flagged as having no reliable reference instead of producing misleading ratios. Performance mattered as well, which is why the data are columnar, results are paginated or streamed, and heavy computations are cached. The traffic-light thresholds are explicit and easy to adjust.

The creative element is the combination of ideas that are rarely seen together in fire tools: a calendar-style heatmap of the full historical record, a month-to-date comparison against a zone-specific norm, a traffic-light status borrowed from risk communication, and the ability to define a study zone just by panning the map, all on top of a single series that unifies two sensors.
